title: Race two urls and give up after a timeout
description: Implement a function called ConfigurableRacer that receives two urls and a timeout duration, requests both urls, and returns the url that responded first together with no error: ConfigurableRacer("http://slow", "http://fast", timeout: 500ms) -> "http://fast", no error. The two urls must be requested at the same time rather than one after the other, so the race takes about as long as the quicker url rather than the sum of both. Have each request run as its own concurrently running task that signals the collecting code when its url has replied; the signal carries no value, so use the smallest possible message type for it, and remember that a channel has to be built before it can be used. The collecting code then waits on both signals at once and takes whichever arrives first. If neither url replies within the timeout, give up and return an empty winner and an error: ConfigurableRacer("http://slow", "http://slow", timeout: 10ms) -> "", error. Do not block forever waiting for a reply. Then implement a second function called Racer that receives just two urls and races them the same way with a fixed timeout of ten seconds, so that callers who do not care about the timeout do not have to supply one.
objective: Practice waiting on several channels at once and adding a timeout so a race can never block forever.

title: Test a racer against fake http servers
description: A function called ConfigurableRacer is already implemented. It receives two urls and a timeout duration, requests both at the same time, and returns the url that replied first together with no error. If neither url replies within the timeout it returns an empty winner and an error. Write tests for it without touching the real internet: stand up throwaway local http servers whose handlers wait a chosen amount of time before replying, and race those servers' own urls. Shut each server down once its test is finished, keeping the shutdown next to the line that started it. Cover both behaviours. First, that the quicker url wins: race a server that replies immediately against one that waits, with a timeout generous enough for both, and assert the immediate server's url comes back with no error. Second, that a race gives up: race servers that all wait longer than the timeout you pass in, and assert an error comes back. Keep the delays and timeouts small so the tests stay fast. Report helpful failures showing the url you got versus the one you wanted.
objective: Practice testing concurrent, time-sensitive code against controllable fake http servers instead of real ones.
mutant_hints: never gives up, so it waits for a reply however long that takes instead of reporting a timeout
reports the slower url as the winner
reports a winner and no error even when nothing replied in time
